Whereinto
whare-in-too'
adv. (into which; an archaic relative of the Authorized Version, used of the land Caleb entered and of the boat the disciples took)
A compound of where and into, on the old English pattern that produced wherein, whereof, whereby, whereunto — a relative adverb standing for into which. The pattern is Germanic and was still ordinary written English in 1611.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The word is a plain relative — into which — and its most important occurrence rewards the reader who slows down for it. Of Caleb, after ten spies had brought back an evil report and the congregation had wept all night: “But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully, him will I bring into the land whereinto he went; and his seed shall possess it” (Numbers 14:24). The precision is the point. Caleb had walked over that ground with the other spies; he had seen the same giants and the same walled cities; and God promises that the very land he entered as a scout he will possess as an inheritance. Two things are said of him and they belong together: another spirit and followed me fully. The generation that would not go in had seen God's glory and His miracles in Egypt and in the wilderness and had tempted Him ten times (Numbers 14:22). Forty-five years later Joshua repeats the promise as fact (Joshua 14:9). John uses the same word of a boat: the crowd saw “that one whereinto his disciples were entered” (John 6:22).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines whereinto as into which, and lists it among the compound relative adverbs of older English.

expand to see more

WHEREINTO, adv. Into which.

The doors whereinto they entered.

WHEREIN, adv. In which; as the house wherein he lives.

2. In what; in which thing, time, respect or the like.

WHEREUNTO, adv. To what; to which; used relatively or interrogatively.

Key Scripture

Numbers 14:24 — "But my servant Caleb, because he had another spirit with him, and hath followed me fully, him will I bring into the land whereinto he went; and his seed shall possess it."

Numbers 14:22 — "Because all those men which have seen my glory, and my miracles, which I did in Egypt and in the wilderness, and have tempted me now these ten times, and have not hearkened to my voice;"

Joshua 14:9 — "And Moses sware on that day, saying, Surely the land whereon thy feet have trodden shall be thine inheritance, and thy children's for ever, because thou hast wholly followed the LORD my God."

John 6:22 — "The day following, when the people which stood on the other side of the sea saw that there was none other boat there, save that one whereinto his disciples were entered, and that Jesus went not with his disciples into the boat, but that his disciples were gone away alone;"

Modern Corruption

Caleb's another spirit is read as natural optimism, when Scripture presents it as something God gave and God names.

expand to see more

The usual application of Numbers 14 makes Caleb the positive thinker and the ten spies the pessimists, so that the lesson becomes a matter of attitude. The text is careful to say something else. God says Caleb had another spirit with him and had followed me fully — the first a possession, the second a course of action, and both spoken by God as His own assessment. Caleb had not seen a smaller enemy; his own speech grants the giants and the cities and answers them with if the LORD delight in us. Faith in Scripture is never the underestimation of a difficulty; it is the accurate weighing of a difficulty against a promise.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the word itself. The principle to recover is the specificity of the reward. God does not say He will bring Caleb into a land but into the land whereinto he went — the ground he had walked on the reconnaissance, which he later asked for by name: give me this mountain, Hebron, where the Anakim were. Forty-five years of wandering he had not caused stood between the promise and the possession, and he asked for the hardest portion at eighty-five. The generation that refused died in the wilderness, and their children inherited what their fathers would not take.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew asher ba shammah, “which he went thither” — Numbers 14:24; ruach acheret, another spirit; male achar, to follow fully; Greek eis ho, into which — John 6:22.

expand to see more

Hebrew ruach acheret — another spirit; Numbers 14:24, God's own account of Caleb.

Hebrew male achar — to fill up after, to follow fully; the phrase repeated of Caleb six times.

Hebrew nachalah — an inheritance; Joshua 14:9, the promise made fact.

Greek eis ho — into which; the construction John 6:22 uses of the boat.

English where- compounds — wherein, whereof, whereby, whereunto — ordinary written English in 1611.

Usage

"“The land whereinto he went” — the very ground he scouted, given as inheritance."

"“Because he had another spirit with him” — God's assessment, not a temperament."

"“Have tempted me now these ten times” — what the other generation had seen and done."
